paragraphs.heading: What an arachnid is
paragraphs.text: Arachnids are arthropods that make up the class Arachnida, within the subphylum Chelicerata. The class takes in spiders and scorpions, ticks and mites, harvestmen, pseudoscorpions and several less familiar groups. More than 110,000 species have been named, and 51,000 of them are spiders. The name comes from the Greek word for spider, aráchnē, after the myth of Arachne, a proud human weaver who was turned into a spider.

paragraphs.heading: Eight legs and more
paragraphs.text: Almost all adult arachnids have eight legs, while adult insects all have six. Unlike insects, arachnids also have no antennae and no wings. They do carry two extra pairs of appendages. The first pair, the chelicerae, are used in feeding and defense, and the second, the pedipalps, may help with feeding, moving about or reproduction. In the Solifugae the palps look so much like legs that these animals seem to have ten.

paragraphs.heading: Two body sections
paragraphs.text: An arachnid's body has two sections, the prosoma and the opisthosoma, also known as the cephalothorax and the abdomen. Those second names are questioned. Cephalothorax suggests a head joined to a thorax, yet no fossil or embryo evidence shows that arachnids ever had a separate thorax. The front section is usually covered by a single carapace without segments. Apart from the spinnerets of spiders and a pair of pectines on scorpions, the abdomen carries no appendages.

paragraphs.heading: Straightening a leg
paragraphs.text: Like every arthropod, an arachnid has an exoskeleton, and it also has an inner support of cartilage-like tissue, the endosternite, where certain muscles attach. Most arachnids lack the muscles that would straighten the outer joints of their limbs. Spiders and whip scorpions push their limbs straight with the pressure of their hemolymph. Solifuges and some harvestmen extend their knees using very elastic thickenings in the joint cuticle.

paragraphs.heading: Made for land
paragraphs.text: Almost all living arachnids live on land, although some live in fresh water, and some in the sea everywhere except the pelagic zone. Several traits suit them to life on land. They breathe through internal surfaces such as tracheae, or through book lungs, an internal series of thin vascular plates that swap gases with the air. Other land adaptations include limbs suited to walking on land, internal fertilisation, special sense organs, and a waxy layer on the cuticle that, together with efficient excretory organs, helps save water.

paragraphs.heading: Waste and blood
paragraphs.text: Arachnids get rid of waste through coxal glands along the sides of the prosoma, Malpighian tubules that empty into the gut, or both. Their main nitrogen waste is guanine. What their blood contains depends on how they breathe. Arachnids with an efficient tracheal system do not need their blood to carry oxygen and may have a reduced circulation. In scorpions and some spiders, however, the blood holds haemocyanin, a copper-based pigment that does a job similar to haemoglobin in vertebrates.
